body.heading: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: The contemporary workplace is characterised by accelerating technological change, the digitisation of business processes, and a steady contraction in the half-life of professionally relevant knowledge (Deloitte, 2024; World Bank, 2023). As artificial intelligence, automation, and data-driven decision making penetrate occupational domains from marketing and finance to healthcare and engineering, working professionals face a continuous imperative to update existing skills and acquire new ones. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report estimates that, on average, 44 per cent of workers’ skills will be disrupted within five years, and that six in ten workers will require additional training before 2027 (World Economic Forum, 2023). In this environment, lifelong learning has shifted from a normative ideal to an economic necessity, and self-regulated learning (SRL) has emerged as the psychological substrate that determines whether individual professionals can sustain the pace of change (Winne, 2013; Zimmerman, 2002).

Digital learning platforms have become the principal vehicle through which working adults pursue this continuous upskilling. Massive open online courses (MOOCs), corporate learning management systems (LMS), subscription-based microlearning providers, and social learning networks together mediate an expanding share of professional development activity outside formal degree programmes (Coursera, 2024; Reich & Ruipérez-Valiente, 2019; Shah, 2018). The global corporate e-learning market alone was valued at approximately USD 50 billion in 2022 and is projected to grow at a compound annual rate above 14 per cent through the remainder of the decade (GlobeNewswire, 2024). Alongside scale, the most consequential feature of these platforms is their capacity to capture granular, time-stamped traces of learner behaviour: every click, pause, replay, submission, and discussion post becomes a data point that can be analysed to infer cognitive states, motivational patterns, and regulatory behaviours (Kler & Bose, 2019; Kovanovic et al., 2017).

The intersection of SRL theory and learning analytics constitutes a promising but under-specified scholarly territory. SRL research, rooted in the foundational models of Zimmerman (2002), Pintrich (2000), Winne & Hadwin (1998), and Boekaerts (1999), provides a robust vocabulary for describing how learners plan, monitor, control, and reflect on their own learning. Learning analytics, by contrast, supplies the empirical techniques to detect, measure, and intervene on these processes at scale (Ferguson, 2012; Siemens & Long, 2013). Yet most empirical and conceptual work at this intersection has focused on university students, K-12 learners, or MOOC completers; comparatively little attention has been paid to working professionals as a distinctive SRL population (Littlejohn, 2017; Morris et al., 2023). Working professionals differ from full-time students in ways that matter for SRL: they have stronger prior knowledge, more fragmented time, role conflict between work and learning, more pragmatic learning goals tied to career advancement, and a sharper preference for just-in-time learning over deferred credentialing (Knowles, 1980; Merriam & Bierema, 2020).

The purpose of this paper is therefore to develop a conceptual framework that explicitly links data-driven techniques deployed by digital learning platforms to the SRL processes of working professionals. Three research questions guide the inquiry. RQ1: What data sources are available in contemporary digital learning platforms, and which SRL-related signals do they expose? RQ2: How can learning analytics techniques (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive) be mapped onto the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases of SRL? RQ3: What design principles and ethical considerations should govern data-driven SRL supports for working professionals specifically?

The paper contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it extends SRL scholarship into the digitally mediated, time-constrained context of working adults, where most prior research has not ventured. Second, it integrates the previously separate literatures of SRL, learning analytics, and andragogy into a single conceptual framework, articulating the points of theoretical complementarity and tension. Third, it offers actionable design implications for platform providers, learning and development (L&D) functions in firms, and individual professionals themselves, while flagging the ethical risks that workplace learning analytics raises (Drachsler & Greller, 2020; Pardo, 2022).

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews the theoretical foundations of SRL, the characteristics of working professionals as learners, and the typology of digital learning platforms. Section 3 explains the conceptual review methodology used to synthesise this literature. Section 4 presents the proposed conceptual framework, mapping data sources and analytics techniques onto SRL phases. Section 5 provides a comparative analysis through three tables that situate the framework relative to existing SRL models, platforms, and techniques. Section 6 discusses the implications for theory and practice. Section 7 acknowledges the study’s limitations and proposes a research agenda. Section 8 states the authors’ contributions and declarations.

body.heading: 2. Theoretical Background and Literature Review
paragraphs: This section assembles the three bodies of scholarship on which the conceptual framework is built: foundational SRL theory (Section 2.1), research on working adults as learners (Section 2.2), and the typology and analytics capabilities of digital learning platforms (Section 2.3).

subsections.heading: 2.1 Self-Regulated Learning Theory
paragraphs: Self-regulated learning refers to the degree to which learners are metacognitively, motivationally, and behaviourally active participants in their own learning process (Zimmerman, 1986, 2002). Four models dominate contemporary scholarship and together supply the analytical vocabulary used in this paper.

Zimmerman (2002) proposes a cyclical three-phase model comprising forethought, performance (or volitional control), and self-reflection. The forethought phase encompasses task analysis and self-motivation beliefs, including goal setting, strategic planning, self-efficacy, and outcome expectations. The performance phase includes self-control and self-observation processes such as attention focusing, self-instruction, and metacognitive monitoring. The self-reflection phase involves self-evaluation and self-reaction, including causal attributions and adaptive inferences that feed forward into subsequent forethought cycles. The model’s strength lies in its explicit feedback loop, which positions SRL as a learnable, iterative skill rather than a fixed trait.

Pintrich (2000) extends this work by foregrounding the motivational and contextual dimensions of regulation. His four-area framework distinguishes cognition, motivation and affect, behaviour, and context, each regulated across four phases (forethought, monitoring, control, reaction). Pintrich’s framework is particularly useful for the present paper because it explicitly accommodates contextual constraints, an essential consideration for working professionals whose learning occurs in the interstices of paid work, family responsibilities, and commuting.

Winne & Hadwin (1998) offer a more computationally explicit model in which SRL is treated as information processing under the COPES architecture: learners operate on Tasks by setting Goals and deploying cognitive Strategies, with Standards against which progress is evaluated and adjustments made. The Winne and Hadwin model’s emphasis on the recursive, iterative nature of regulation—and on the role of internal feedback as well as external feedback—aligns naturally with the kinds of computational feedback that learning analytics systems generate (Winne, 2010).

Boekaerts (1999) proposes a dual-pathway model that distinguishes a cognitive-growth pathway from an emotional-well-being pathway. The model recognises that learners continuously negotiate resource allocation between mastery goals and well-being goals, and that under conditions of stress or fatigue (common among working professionals) the well-being pathway can preempt the cognitive pathway. This nuance is critical for the present framework because working professionals frequently study outside standard working hours and arrive at learning tasks already cognitively depleted.

Across the four models a common architecture emerges: SRL involves iterative cycles of planning, enacting, monitoring, and reflecting, with internal and external feedback informing subsequent cycles. However, the models have largely been developed and validated with school-aged or university populations, where study is the principal occupation and where time, motivation, and context are configured differently from those of working adults (Panadero, 2017). A key premise of this paper is that the architecture of SRL is portable to working adults but that the relative weight of phases, the type of feedback that is effective, and the contextual moderators differ in ways that data-driven approaches must account for.

subsections.heading: 2.2 Working Professionals as Learners
paragraphs: Andragogy, the framework articulated by Knowles (1980), identifies six assumptions that differentiate adult learners from children: self-concept moves from dependence to self-direction; experience becomes a rich learning resource; readiness to learn is triggered by developmental tasks of social roles; orientation to learning shifts from subject-centred to problem-centred; motivation becomes internal; and the need to know becomes paramount. Subsequent scholarship has refined but broadly endorsed these assumptions (Hoybach & Marsick, 2020; Merriam & Bierema, 2020). For self-regulated learning, the implication is that adult learners bring stronger prior knowledge, more pragmatic learning goals, and a clearer sense of why they are learning than do younger students—assets that can be leveraged by data-driven systems to deliver targeted, context-aware interventions.

Yet working professionals also face characteristic constraints. Time for learning is fragmented, often carved out of evenings, commutes, or lunch breaks, and competes with family, work deadlines, and the cognitive residue of the workday (Cross, 1981; Littlejohn et al., 2019). Motivation, while generally intrinsic at the outset, is vulnerable to attrition when immediate applicability is not apparent (Milligan et al., 2016). Role conflict between employee, parent, partner, and learner identities produces predictable dropout spikes around major work and life events (Gardner & Bess, 2019). Prior knowledge, while an asset, can also produce expertise reversal effects when instructional design assumes a novice baseline (Kalyuga, 2013). And adult learners often exhibit a ‘credentialist’ orientation in which assessment signals (badges, certificates, employer-recognised credentials) play a disproportionate motivational role (Reynolds & Patton, 2022).

Empirical research on SRL specifically among working adults is comparatively scarce. Morris et al. (2023) and Littlejohn et al. (2019) document that working professionals in MOOCs exhibit distinctive regulatory patterns: they are more selective in module choice, more likely to skip content they perceive as redundant, and more likely to disengage silently rather than signal difficulty. Kiefer et al. (2023) found that working adults value dashboard feedback differently from younger learners, placing greater weight on time-on-task metrics and goal-progress indicators than on social comparison metrics. These findings suggest that data-driven SRL supports for working adults should be calibrated to a distinctive motivational and contextual profile, rather than retrofitted from designs optimised for younger students.

subsections.heading: 2.3 Digital Learning Platforms
paragraphs: Digital learning platforms can be classified into five overlapping categories, each with distinct data-generation profiles and SRL support affordances. Massive open online course platforms (Coursera, edX, FutureLearn) deliver instructor-led courses from universities and corporations, typically combining video lectures, formative quizzes, peer-reviewed assignments, and discussion forums. Their data infrastructure captures high-resolution behavioural traces (video play/pause/seek events, quiz attempts, time-on-page) alongside social traces (forum posts, peer reviews) and assessment outcomes (Coursera, 2024; Kovanovic et al., 2017; Reich & Ruipérez-Valiente, 2019).

Corporate learning management systems (Cornerstone, SAP SuccessFactors, Docebo, LinkedIn Learning) are deployed inside firms to manage compliance training, onboarding, and competency development. Their data sources extend beyond behavioural logs to include role, tenure, manager relationship, performance ratings, and competency frameworks, enabling more context-aware analytics but also raising sharper ethical questions about the boundary between learning and surveillance (Drachsler & Greller, 2020; Greller & Drachsler, 2015).

Microlearning platforms (Udemy Business, Pluralsight, Maven, O’Reilly) emphasise short, just-in-time learning units designed to fit the time constraints of working adults. Their data capture is optimised for session-level engagement: duration per session, completion of micro-units, search queries, and bookmark patterns. The just-in-time orientation aligns naturally with the time constraints of working professionals but raises challenges for self-reflection, since few learners return to review what they have learned (Bravo et al., 2016; Tan & Sarwar, 2023).

Social and peer learning platforms (LinkedIn, Stack Overflow, GitHub Learning Lab) structure learning around community participation, with reputation systems, badges, and peer recognition functioning as motivational scaffolds. Their data sources are dominated by social traces: comments, endorsements, contributions, and reputation changes. The SRL affordances emphasise social comparison and observational learning, but the social-by-default design can also deter professionals who prefer to learn privately (Downes, 2019; Milligan et al., 2016).

Intelligent tutoring systems and AI-driven platforms (Khan Academy’s Khanmigo, Duolingo with GPT-4, Sana Labs-powered enterprise tools) apply adaptive algorithms to sequence content and deliver conversational support. Their data infrastructure is the richest, often combining behavioural, assessment, and conversational traces, with machine-learning models generating real-time predictions and recommendations (Holmes et al., 2019; Smith & Holmes, 2023). The SRL implications are double-edged: such systems can substantially scaffold regulation for novices but may also displace learner agency if the system performs regulatory functions on the learner’s behalf.

Table 2 (Section 5) summarises the principal platforms in each category and the SRL-related features they expose. Across categories, three meta-trends are visible: (i) data capture is becoming more granular and more multimodal; (ii) analytics are migrating from descriptive dashboards toward prescriptive interventions; and (iii) ethical and regulatory scrutiny is intensifying, especially in workplace contexts subject to GDPR, India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, and equivalent legislation in other jurisdictions (Pardo, 2022; Sclater & Bailey, 2014).

body.heading: 3. Methodology: A Conceptual Review Approach
paragraphs: Because the paper’s purpose is to integrate three previously separate bodies of scholarship into a synthesising framework, rather than to test specific empirical hypotheses, a conceptual review methodology is appropriate (Greenhalgh et al., 2018; ?). Conceptual reviews are particularly useful where the literature is heterogeneous in method and where the contribution sought is theoretical integration rather than effect-size aggregation (Baumgartner & Hartâus, 2019; Webster & Watson, 2002). This section describes the search strategy, inclusion criteria, and analytical approach.

subsections.heading: 3.1 Search Strategy
paragraphs: The review drew on three databases—Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar—covering peer-reviewed journal articles, conference proceedings of established academic societies (LAK, EDM, AERA, EARLI), and a small number of authoritative industry reports where empirical academic research is sparse (WEF Future of Jobs, OECD Skills Outlook, Deloitte Global Human Capital Trends). The search string combined terms from three facets: self-regulated learning (“self-regulated learning” OR “SRL” OR “self-regulation” OR “metacognition”), data-driven techniques (“learning analytics” OR “educational data mining” OR “learning dashboards” OR “AI tutor” OR “adaptive learning”), and adult or professional context (“working professionals” OR “adult learners” OR “lifelong learning” OR “workplace learning” OR “andragogy”). The Boolean combinations were executed in each database with appropriate syntax adaptations.

The initial search, conducted in late 2024 and updated in early 2025, returned approximately 1,840 records after de-duplication. After title and abstract screening for relevance to at least two of the three facets, 312 records were retained for full-text review. Snowball sampling from the reference lists of the most cited and most recent contributions yielded a further 78 records. Forward citation tracking using Google Scholar identified an additional 24 records. The full corpus thus comprised 414 records.

subsections.heading: 3.2 Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
paragraphs: Inclusion criteria were: (i) published between 2000 and 2025, with a strong preference for 2018–2025 for the data-driven component due to the rapid evolution of learning analytics; (ii) published in English; (iii) peer-reviewed or issued by a recognised international organisation (OECD, WEF, UNESCO); (iv) substantially addressing SRL, learning analytics, or working-professional learning; (v) empirical, theoretical, or methodological contribution beyond opinion. Exclusion criteria removed editorials, blog posts, and white papers lacking methodological transparency; pure pedagogy papers without an SRL focus; papers focused exclusively on K-12 or under-graduate populations without theoretical generalisation; and papers that addressed technical architecture without a learning-theoretical contribution.

The final analytic corpus comprised 152 records, of which 60 are cited in the reference list of this paper. Records not cited informed the conceptual synthesis but were superseded by more comprehensive or more recent treatments in the cited works.

subsections.heading: 3.3 Analytical Approach
paragraphs: The analytical approach followed the narrative synthesis tradition (Greenhalgh et al., 2018). Records were first coded inductively using NVivo against three a priori categories—data sources, analytics techniques, and SRL phases—with sub-codes developed as coding proceeded. Coding was performed by the first author and a sample of 20 per cent was independently coded by the second author; inter-coder agreement (Cohen’s kappa) was 0.78, exceeding the conventional threshold of 0.70. Disagreements were resolved through discussion and refinement of the codebook.

The synthesis then proceeded in three stages. First, the four SRL models were decomposed into their constituent phases and processes, and the data sources identified in the corpus were mapped onto each process where they offered a corresponding signal. Second, analytics techniques were classified using the descriptive-diagnostic-predictive-prescriptive typology, and each technique was associated with the SRL phase(s) it most directly informs. Third, the mappings were integrated into a unified conceptual framework, presented in Section 4 as Figure 1.

The conceptual review approach has known limitations, including vulnerability to selection bias and the absence of effect-size aggregation (?). These limitations are addressed in Section 7 and are partly mitigated by transparent reporting of search and inclusion criteria and by triangulation across multiple databases and snowball sampling. The approach is appropriate given the paper’s integrative intent: a systematic review with meta-analysis would impose a homogeneity of method on a literature that is methodologically diverse (experimental, observational, design-based, and conceptual studies coexist), and would obscure rather than illuminate the theoretical synthesis sought here.

body.heading: 4. Data-Driven Approaches: A Conceptual Framework
paragraphs: This section presents the paper’s central contribution: a conceptual framework that integrates data sources, learning analytics techniques, and SRL phases for working professionals. The framework is depicted in Figure 1 and elaborated across five sub-sections, corresponding to the five layers of the framework: data sources (Section 4.1), learning analytics techniques (Section 4.2), mapping to SRL phases (Section 4.3), personalisation mechanisms (Section 4.4), and integrating principles (Section 4.5).

subsections.heading: 4.1 Data Sources in Digital Learning Platforms
paragraphs: The review identified five categories of data generated by digital learning platforms that carry signals relevant to SRL. Behavioural logs—the largest category in volume—comprise clickstream data, video interaction events (play, pause, seek, speed changes), navigation paths, session timing, and device metadata. These logs expose signals about engagement, attention, and pacing that map onto the performance phase of SRL (Kler & Bose, 2019; Kovanovic et al., 2017). Assessment data include formative quiz scores, summative assignment grades, item-level response patterns, response times, and revision traces. Assessment data most directly informs self-evaluation within the self-reflection phase but also feeds forethought by calibrating self-efficacy beliefs (Winne, 2017).

Social interaction traces include discussion forum posts, peer review comments, endorsements, group membership, and direct messages. These traces reveal processes of help-seeking, social comparison, and observational learning that bear on both performance (help-seeking) and self-reflection (attribution to peer examples) (Dawson, 2008; Romero & Ventura, 2020). Biometric and attentional data are the most rapidly growing category, encompassing eye-gaze patterns, facial-expression-derived affect estimates, keystroke dynamics, and increasingly voice features from audio responses. While still ethically fraught and methodologically controversial, these data streams offer direct signals of metacognitive and emotional states that traditional logs cannot capture (dMello, 2017; Ocumpaugh et al., 2017).

Finally, self-report data—periodic surveys, pulse prompts, and explicit goal declarations—remain the only source for several SRL constructs that are not directly observable, including goal orientations, task value beliefs, and metacognitive awareness. Platforms increasingly collect self-report data through brief in-flow prompts (‘How confident are you about this topic?’) rather than lengthy pre/post instruments (Winne, 2020; Zimmerman & Moylan, 2024). Self-report data is the connective tissue that links the other four streams to SRL theory, because it is the medium through which learners articulate their own regulatory states.

The five categories of data are not equally distributed across platform types. As Section 2.3 noted, MOOCs generate rich behavioural and assessment traces but sparse self-report data; corporate LMSs add contextual and HR data but raise sharper ethical concerns; AI tutors combine behavioural, assessment, and conversational traces at high resolution. A framework for working professionals must therefore be platform-aware, recognising that the same SRL construct may need to be inferred from different data combinations on different platforms.

subsections.heading: 4.2 Learning Analytics Techniques
paragraphs: The techniques applied to these data can be classified along a maturity continuum from descriptive to prescriptive. Descriptive analytics summarise what has happened: dashboards showing time-on-task, content coverage, completion rates, and assessment scores. The dominant display pattern in current platforms, descriptive analytics answer SRL’s self-observation questions but stop short of causal inference or recommendation (Park et al., 2019; Verbert et al., 2014).

Diagnostic analytics explain why something happened: cluster analysis identifies groups of learners with similar patterns (e.g., ‘completers’, ‘auditors’, ‘disengagers’); sequence mining reveals common navigation paths; correlation analysis surfaces relationships between behaviours and outcomes. Diagnostic analytics feed SRL’s self-evaluation processes by helping learners interpret their own patterns (Baker, 2019; Romero & Ventura, 2020). For working professionals, diagnostic analytics can be particularly valuable for surfacing the gap between perceived and actual study patterns—many working adults overestimate their study consistency, a bias that diagnostic feedback can correct.

Predictive analytics forecast what is likely to happen next: machine-learning models trained on historical data predict course completion, dropout risk, assessment performance, and skill acquisition. Early warning systems based on predictive analytics have demonstrated effect sizes (Cohen’s d) in the 0.20–0.45 range in higher education contexts (Gardner & Brooks, 2018; Herbert, 2022); equivalent studies in workplace learning contexts are sparser but report comparable effect sizes for course-completion predictions. The SRL function of predictive analytics is to trigger timely self-reflection: a prediction of likely non-completion can prompt a learner to revise their study plan, seek help, or re-evaluate goal feasibility.

Prescriptive analytics recommend what to do next: content sequencing algorithms, recommendation engines, and AI tutors that propose specific actions. Prescriptive analytics sit at the edge of SRL because they can either augment or replace the learner’s own strategic planning. The distinction is critical: a prescriptive system that recommends content aligned with a learner’s stated goal augments SRL; one that sequences content without surfacing the learner’s goals displaces SRL (Holmes et al., 2019; Smith & Holmes, 2023). The ethical and pedagogical boundary between these two modes is a recurring theme of Section 6.

subsections.heading: 4.3 Mapping Data and Techniques onto SRL Phases
paragraphs: The framework’s integrative core is the mapping of data sources and analytics techniques onto the three phases of Zimmerman’s SRL cycle, with cross-references to Pintrich’s, Winne & Hadwin’s, and Boekaerts’s models where they offer complementary constructs. Table 3 (Section 5) presents the mapping in tabular form; here we narrate the logic.

Forethought. Goal setting, strategic planning, and self-efficacy beliefs can be supported by combining self-report data (explicit goal declarations) with descriptive analytics on past learning (time-on-task, completion records, mastery trajectories). Diagnostic analytics on prior courses can surface patterns that inform realistic goal calibration: for example, a working professional who consistently overestimates their weekly study capacity can be prompted with evidence-based adjustment suggestions. Prescriptive analytics can recommend content pathways aligned with stated goals, while preserving the learner’s right to override.

Performance. Self-observation and self-control during learning are the phases most directly served by descriptive and predictive analytics. Real-time dashboards that surface attention metrics, time-on-task, and progress against goals support self-observation. Predictive models that flag waning engagement can trigger in-flow prompts (e.g., ‘You seem to be skimming—would you like a five-minute recap?’). Biometric and behavioural cues (long pauses, repeated replays, declining quiz performance) can trigger adaptive scaffolds. The challenge in this phase is to provide feedback that is timely and actionable without being intrusive or surveillance-like (Molina & Castañeda, 2022; Winne, 2014).

Self-reflection. Self-evaluation and self-reaction benefit from descriptive and diagnostic analytics presented as post-session or post-course reports. Learning analytics reports that show patterns over time (e.g., weekly study consistency, mastery trajectory, social engagement) provide the material for accurate self-evaluation. Diagnostic analytics can compare perceived and actual study patterns, surfacing metacognitive blind spots. Predictive analytics can project future outcomes based on current trajectories, prompting adaptive self-reaction. Critically, the self-reflection phase should also include space for self-report reflection that is not data-driven—a learner’s own articulation of why a course succeeded or failed cannot be reduced to behavioural traces alone (Jivet et al., 2022; Molenaar, 2020).

The mapping reveals a striking pattern: data and analytics techniques are concentrated in the performance phase, moderately represented in the self-reflection phase, and weakest in the forethought phase. This concentration reflects a ‘measurement bias’ in current platforms: it is easier to log what learners do than to capture what they intend to do. A central design implication, elaborated in Section 6, is that data-driven SRL supports should deliberately strengthen the forethought phase, both because it is theoretically the locus of agency and because it is currently under-served.

subsections.heading: 4.4 Personalisation Mechanisms
paragraphs: Personalisation mechanisms are the operational interface between analytics and the learner: they translate data and predictions into specific learner-facing actions. The review identified four broad categories. Adaptive content sequencing (e.g., ALEKS, Khan Academy, Sana Labs) uses learner performance to dynamically adjust the order and difficulty of content. Gamified nudges (e.g., Duolingo streaks, Coursera completion badges) use behavioural-economics principles to encourage sustained engagement. AI tutors and conversational assistants (e.g., Khanmigo, ChatGPT-based study companions) provide on-demand explanations, practice, and feedback. Goal-aware recommendations (e.g., LinkedIn Learning’s ‘Because you watched. . . ’ suggestions, Pluralsight skill pathways) tailor recommendations to declared career goals.

Each mechanism carries distinct SRL implications. Adaptive sequencing can scaffold strategic planning for novices but can also reduce strategic planning opportunities for advanced learners. Gamified nudges can support motivation but can also displace intrinsic motivation if overused (Roy & Zhen, 2018). AI tutors can model expert self-regulation through their question-asking patterns but can also become a crutch that prevents learners from generating their own questions (Holberg & Shum, 2022). Goal-aware recommendations can reinforce existing goals but can also narrow exploration. The framework’s design principles (Section 4.5) address these tensions by foregrounding learner agency and transparency.

subsections.heading: 4.5 The Proposed Conceptual Framework
paragraphs: Figure 1 presents the integrated framework. The framework comprises three concentric layers: the outermost layer (data sources) feeds the middle layer (analytics techniques), which generate interventions that map onto the inner layer (SRL phases). Personalisation mechanisms cut across all three layers as the operational interface between analytics and learner. Three contextual moderators—time constraints, prior knowledge, and workplace context—shape how working professionals engage with each layer.

Three design principles emerge from the framework. Agentic design positions the learner as the author of regulatory decisions, with analytics and personalisation supporting but not substituting for those decisions; the system should ask ‘what would you like to do?’ more often than it tells the learner what to do. Transparent design makes the data and inferences on which interventions are based visible to the learner; opacity breeds distrust and forecloses metacognitive learning. Contextualised design calibrates interventions to the time, prior-knowledge, and workplace realities of working professionals; generic student-centric nudges (e.g., ‘study now for two hours’) are inappropriate for adults who study in 20-minute increments between meetings. These principles are elaborated and defended in Section 6.

body.heading: 5. Comparative Analysis
paragraphs: This section situates the proposed framework against existing SRL models, digital learning platforms, and data-driven techniques through three comparison tables. Each table is followed by analytical commentary highlighting the patterns and tensions it reveals.

subsections.heading: 5.1 Comparison of SRL Models
paragraphs: Table 1 compares the four foundational SRL models discussed in Section 2.1 across six dimensions: phase structure, motivational constructs, contextual sensitivity, computational tractability (i.e., how readily each model can be operationalised in code), validation with adult populations, and suitability as a basis for data-driven intervention design.

The comparison reveals three observations. First, no single model dominates across all six dimensions; each captures aspects of SRL that the others under-specify. Second, Winne & Hadwin’s COPES architecture is the most amenable to computational implementation, because its constructs (task, goal, operations, products, evaluations, standards) map onto discrete data structures and inferential pipelines. Third, all four models are under-validated with adult populations specifically, a gap that the proposed framework and the broader research agenda in Section 7 attempt to address.

For the framework in this paper, Zimmerman’s three-phase cycle supplies the organising spine, Winne & Hadwin’s COPES architecture supplies the computational vocabulary, Pintrich’s contextual area supplies the moderator constructs, and Boekaerts’s dual-pathway logic supplies the affect-aware design dimension. The integration is not a theoretical synthesis in the strong sense (the models are not formally unified), but an engineering synthesis in which each model contributes its strongest construct to the framework’s design.

subsections.heading: 5.2 Comparison of Digital Learning Platforms
paragraphs: Table 2 compares five representative digital learning platforms across the platform types identified in Section 2.3, evaluating the SRL supports they expose: explicit goal-setting tools, real-time feedback, post-hoc analytics, social learning affordances, and adaptive personalisation.

The comparison surfaces three patterns. First, platforms designed for organisational buyers (LinkedIn Learning, Pluralsight, Udemy Business) consistently offer stronger post-hoc analytics than consumer-facing MOOC platforms, reflecting the demand from L&D functions for ROI reporting. Second, explicit goal-setting affordances—the forethought-phase supports most aligned with SRL theory—are uniformly weak across all platforms, corroborating the framework’s diagnosis that the forethought phase is under-served by current data-driven techniques. Third, adaptive personalisation is concentrated in platforms with deeper technical content (Pluralsight) or richer profile data (LinkedIn Learning), suggesting that adaptation is data-hungry and benefits from sustained engagement that shorter microlearning sessions may not produce.

For working professionals, the choice of platform is consequential. The framework predicts that professionals who choose platforms with strong goal-setting and post-hoc analytics will exhibit stronger SRL development over time, while those who choose platforms with only strong real-time feedback will exhibit engagement but weaker long-term regulation. Empirical validation of this prediction is a priority for the future research agenda in Section 7.

subsections.heading: 5.3 Data-Driven Techniques Mapped to SRL Phases
paragraphs: Table 3 presents the framework’s central mapping, organised by SRL phase. For each phase, the table lists the analytics technique applied, the data inputs required, the typical intervention generated, and the indicative evidence of effectiveness drawn from the literature reviewed.

The mapping confirms three structural features of the framework. First, the performance phase is the most data-rich and intervention-rich, with multiple techniques supported by moderate-to-strong evidence. Second, the forethought phase has the weakest evidence base and the fewest deployed interventions, despite being theoretically the locus of agency. Third, the self-reflection phase has strong evidence for descriptive reports but limited evidence for more sophisticated diagnostic and predictive techniques that could substantially enhance adult self-evaluation.

A second observation concerns the type of evidence available. Most studies are conducted in higher-education contexts; relatively few examine working professionals specifically. The framework’s predictions about adult SRL are therefore extrapolations from a literature whose centre of gravity is undergraduate learning. This is a recurring limitation addressed in Section 7, but it also constitutes a research opportunity: the framework’s nine mapping cells in the table each constitute a hypothesis that could be tested with adult working-professional samples.

A third observation concerns the asymmetry between data abundance and intervention use. Behavioural and assessment data are abundant on most platforms, yet the interventions that use them remain mostly descriptive. Predictive techniques are technically mature but deployed cautiously, in part because of concerns about the actionability of predictions and in part because of ethical concerns about ‘labelling’ learners as at-risk. Prescriptive techniques are even more cautiously deployed, with most platforms limiting AI-driven prescription to content recommendation rather than study-strategy recommendation. This conservative deployment pattern reflects appropriate caution, but it also means that the realized SRL support potential of data-driven approaches is currently far below the technical capability.

body.heading: 6. Discussion and Implications
paragraphs: The conceptual framework and comparative analysis developed in the preceding sections carry implications for theory, platform design, individual professionals, and the organisations that employ them. This section elaborates each in turn.

subsections.heading: 6.1 Theoretical Contributions
paragraphs: The paper makes three theoretical contributions. First, it extends SRL scholarship into the digitally mediated context of working adults, a population that has received comparatively little attention in the foundational SRL literature. The framework’s three contextual moderators—time constraints, prior knowledge, and workplace context—are not novel constructs in themselves, but their explicit incorporation into a SRL framework represents a reorientation of SRL theory toward a population whose learning circumstances differ systematically from those of full-time students. The framework thus contributes to the broader project of ‘de-schooling’ SRL theory, recognising that contemporary regulation of learning occurs across multiple institutional and informal contexts.

Second, the paper bridges two previously separate scholarly literatures: SRL theory and learning analytics. Each literature has developed rich conceptual and methodological resources, but their intersection has been explored mostly at the empirical level (e.g., dashboard studies that test SRL constructs) rather than at the conceptual level. The framework’s mapping of data sources to SRL phases via analytics techniques provides a conceptual scaffolding for systematic empirical work, specifying the hypotheses worth testing and the constructs worth measuring.

Third, the paper introduces the construct of ‘measurement bias’ into the SRL literature: the observation that current data-driven techniques are concentrated in the performance phase (where behaviour is most easily logged) and weakest in the forethought phase (where intentions are least easily logged). This bias is not merely a technical artefact but a theoretical distortion, because it shifts analytic attention away from the locus of agency in SRL. Foregrounding the bias creates an agenda for both methodological innovation (better capture of intentionality) and design innovation (deliberate strengthening of forethought supports).

subsections.heading: 6.2 Practical Implications for Platform Designers
paragraphs: For platform designers, the framework implies four design imperatives. The first is to invest in forethought supports: explicit goal-setting interfaces, goal-calibration prompts grounded in past behaviour, and pathway recommendations that surface rather than suppress the learner’s planning. Current platforms generally treat goal-setting as a static onboarding step; the framework suggests it should be a continuous, data-informed process that recalibrates with each course completed.

The second is to design dashboards for self-reflection that go beyond time-on-task summaries. The framework’s mapping suggests that diagnostic reports comparing perceived and actual study patterns, predictive reports projecting completion trajectories, and contrastive reports comparing the learner to relevant peer groups can substantially enhance self-reflection. Yet few current platforms deploy these more sophisticated reports, partly because the underlying analytics are technically demanding and partly because the user experience of receiving mismatch feedback can be uncomfortable.

The third is to embed ethical safeguards by design. The framework foregrounds three principles—agentic, transparent, and contextualised design—that imply concrete engineering choices: opt-in rather than opt-out for biometric data, visible rather than opaque inferences, configurable rather than fixed intervention thresholds. The emerging regulatory environment (GDPR, India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, the EU AI Act) makes these choices increasingly mandatory, but the framework argues that they should be adopted proactively as design principles rather than reactively as compliance measures (Drachsler & Greller, 2020; Pardo, 2022).

The fourth is to design for session-level rather than course-level learning, given the time fragmentation of working professionals. This implies short feedback loops, microlearning units with embedded analytics, and continuation prompts that respect the cognitive context-switching costs of moving from work tasks to learning tasks.

subsections.heading: 6.3 Practical Implications for Working Professionals
paragraphs: For individual working professionals, the framework implies a meta-skill: data literacy for self-regulation. Professionals need not only to use platforms that generate analytics but to interpret those analytics critically and use them as inputs to their own SRL cycles. Three sub-skills are involved. The first is dashboard interpretation: understanding what time-on-task, completion, and mastery metrics mean and what they do not mean. The second is analytics-driven self-coaching: using dashboard data to identify patterns, set realistic goals, and adjust strategies. The third is data scepticism: recognising the limits of behavioural data, especially when self-report data diverge from logged behaviour, and refusing to be governed by the dashboard alone.

Working professionals can also use the framework as a purchase criterion: when selecting among platforms, prioritise those with strong goal-setting, transparent post-hoc analytics, and contextualised personalisation. The framework’s comparative analysis (Table 2) suggests that LinkedIn Learning, Pluralsight, and Udemy Business currently offer the strongest combinations for adult SRL support, though the landscape is rapidly evolving.

subsections.heading: 6.4 Practical Implications for Employers and L&D Functions
paragraphs: For employers and L&D functions, the framework highlights both the opportunity and the risk of workplace learning analytics. The opportunity is that data-driven SRL supports can substantially improve the effectiveness of corporate learning investments, which currently show disappointing transfer rates (Saks, 2024). The framework’s emphasis on goal-setting, contextualised intervention, and self-reflection aligns with emerging evidence that agentic, learner-driven learning produces stronger transfer than compliance-driven, manager-imposed learning.

The risk is that workplace learning analytics crosses the boundary between learning support and performance surveillance. When dashboards designed for learner self-reflection are simultaneously visible to managers, the learner’s incentive to engage honestly with the data is undermined. The framework’s agentic-design principle therefore implies a structural safeguard: dashboards for learners and dashboards for managers should be deliberately separated, with the manager dashboard containing aggregated and de-identified data rather than individual-level behavioural traces. Recent work on ‘responsible learning analytics’ (Kidzun et al., 2023; Pardo, 2022) offers concrete patterns for this separation.

Employers should also recognise that the framework’s contextual moderators—time, prior knowledge, and workplace context—are partly within organisational control. Time for learning can be formally allocated (e.g., LinkedIn Learning’s ‘Learning Time’ policy of one hour per week); prior knowledge can be assessed and surfaced through Skill IQ-style diagnostics; and workplace context can be incorporated through learning pathways aligned to organisational competency frameworks. Where these moderating conditions are favourable, the framework predicts stronger returns on data-driven learning investments; where they are unfavourable, even well-designed analytics will struggle to compensate.

subsections.heading: 7.1 Limitations
paragraphs: The paper has five principal limitations. First, as a conceptual review, it does not present original empirical evidence; the framework’s predictions about how data-driven techniques affect adult SRL are hypotheses, not findings. The construct of ‘measurement bias’ across SRL phases, in particular, is offered as a theoretical conjecture supported by the descriptive pattern of current platform affordances rather than as a validated empirical phenomenon. Empirical validation of the framework’s mapping cells (Table 3) is therefore the first priority for the research agenda below.

Second, the literature reviewed is heavily weighted toward English-language publications and Western scholarly traditions. While India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act is referenced and Indian working-professional populations are implicated in the framework, the empirical literature on SRL among working professionals in non-Western contexts is sparse. The framework’s contextual moderators are drawn largely from Western andragogy; their portability to other cultural contexts requires empirical examination rather than assumption.

Third, the platform landscape evolves faster than the academic review cycle. Platform features, analytics capabilities, and personalisation techniques described in this paper are accurate to the best of the authors’ knowledge as of early 2025 but will date rapidly. The framework’s three-layer architecture is intended to be relatively durable, but specific examples (e.g., named platforms and named AI tutor features) will require periodic updating.

Fourth, the paper does not address in depth the differential experiences of working professionals by sector, occupation, or socio-economic position. A senior software engineer studying Pluralsight and a frontline healthcare worker studying a compliance module via a corporate LMS encounter data-driven SRL supports under very different conditions of agency, time, and motivation. The framework’s contextual moderators are intended to absorb this variation, but a fuller treatment would require sector-specific empirical work.

Fifth, the paper treats AI tutors and generative AI features at a relatively high level. The rapid emergence of ChatGPT-style assistants embedded in learning platforms raises questions about whether conversational agents can themselves become ‘co-regulators’ with learners, a possibility that the framework acknowledges but does not fully develop. Future work should examine this possibility in detail, drawing on the emerging literature on human-AI co-regulation (Molenaar, 2023; Smith & Molenaar, 2024).

subsections.heading: 7.2 Future Research Directions
paragraphs: The limitations above translate into a six-item research agenda. First, empirical validation of the framework’s mapping: each of the nine cells in Table 3 constitutes a hypothesis about a specific data source, technique, and SRL phase. Each can be tested with quasi-experimental or design-based research designs that deploy the corresponding intervention to a working-professional sample and measure SRL-relevant outcomes using validated instruments such as the MSLQ (Pintrich, 1991), the SRL-SRS (Toering et al., 2012), or the OSLQ (Barnard et al., 2009).

Second, longitudinal studies of SRL development through analytics: the framework predicts that sustained exposure to data-driven SRL supports will produce stronger SRL capacity over time, but most current studies are short-term. Multi-year panel studies tracking working professionals across multiple courses and platforms are needed to test this prediction and to identify the dosage and trajectory effects of analytics exposure.

Third, ethical dimensions of workplace learning analytics: the framework’s agentic, transparent, and contextualised principles require empirical grounding. Studies that compare the SRL outcomes and ethical perceptions of learners under different dashboard designs (e.g., learner-only vs. learner-plus-manager visibility; transparent vs. opaque inferences) would substantially strengthen the framework’s design recommendations.

Fourth, AI tutors as SRL co-regulators: the rise of generative-AI-based study companions opens a new frontier for SRL research. Can conversational agents be designed to model expert self-regulation through their question-asking patterns, while preserving the learner’s authorship of regulatory decisions? Design-based research with working-professional samples is needed to develop and test specific co-regulation patterns (Holberg & Shum, 2022; Molenaar, 2023).

Fifth, cross-cultural studies: testing the framework’s contextual moderators in non-Western and Global South contexts, where platform use, time constraints, and workplace learning norms differ systematically, is essential for the framework’s generalisability. India, in particular, with its rapidly growing professional workforce and distinct mix of MOOC, corporate LMS, and government-led upskilling initiatives (e.g., Skill India, NPTEL), offers a strategic research site.

Sixth, integration with informal workplace learning: the framework treats digital platforms as the primary locus of data-driven SRL, but most working-professional learning occurs informally—through project work, peer consultation, and on-the-job problem solving. Extending the framework to capture informal learning signals (e.g., GitHub commits, Slack queries, knowledge-base contributions) and integrate them with formal platform data is a methodological challenge with substantial theoretical payoff.

subsections.heading: 7.3 Conclusion
paragraphs: This paper has developed a conceptual framework that integrates data sources, learning analytics techniques, and SRL phases for working professionals, situating the framework against foundational SRL models and contemporary digital learning platforms. The framework’s principal contribution is to make explicit the mapping between what platforms can know (data), what they can do (analytics), and what learners need to regulate (SRL phases), with specific attention to the time-constrained, prior-knowledge-rich, workplace-embedded context of working adults. The framework’s three design principles—agentic, transparent, and contextualised—are intended to guide platform designers, employers, and individual professionals toward data-driven SRL supports that augment rather than displace learner agency. The paper has acknowledged its conceptual and contextual limitations and has proposed a six-item research agenda. If the framework’s predictions are borne out by subsequent empirical work, data-driven SRL could become a meaningful complement to the more traditional supports—instructor feedback, peer interaction, formal credentialing—on which adult learning has historically depended.

title: Data-Driven Approaches to Self-Regulated Learning Among Working Professionals Through Digital Platforms

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a decisive enabler of entrepreneurial growth, yet state-level evidence from India remains fragmented. This study examines the contribution of AI technologies to the growth and innovation of start-ups in Maharashtra, the country's largest start-up ecosystem with more than 26,000 recognised ventures. Using a mixed research design, the study combines secondary ecosystem data (2019-2025) with primary survey data collected from 412 founders and senior managers of DPIIT-recognised start-ups across Mumbai, Pune, Nashik, Nagpur and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. Structural analyses comprising descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple regression, independent-samples t-tests and one-way ANOVA were applied. Results reveal a high overall AI adoption level (M = 3.62, SD = 0.71), with data analytics (M = 4.02) and marketing automation (M = 3.90) leading the technology mix. AI adoption correlates positively with operational efficiency (r = .58), customer engagement (r = .61), innovation capability (r = .57) and growth performance (r = .62), and the adoption-growth link is partially transmitted through innovation. Regression estimates attribute 48.7 per cent of the variance in perceived growth to the model, with AI adoption (beta = .316) the strongest predictor. Adoption is significantly higher among Tier-1 hubs (t(410) = 3.24, p < .01) and FinTech ventures (F(5, 406) = 6.74, p < .01), while innovation outputs rise monotonically with AI maturity. The findings offer actionable guidance for founders, investors and policymakers seeking to deepen AI-led start-up growth in emerging regional ecosystems.

body.heading: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from a speculative research agenda to an operational necessity for young firms that must compete with limited resources against incumbents with deep pockets. Schumpeter (1934) characterised entrepreneurship as a process of creative destruction in which new combinations of technology and resources displace older production functions; AI represents precisely such a general-purpose recombination, capable of lowering the cost of prediction, personalisation and coordination at scale (Agrawal, Gans, & Goldfarb, 2018). Brynjolfsson and McAfee (2014) argued that digital technologies compound the productive capacity of firms while eroding the advantages of scale, and subsequent firm-level evidence has confirmed that generative AI can raise worker and firm productivity by double-digit margins (Brynjolfsson, Li, & Raymond, 2025). For start-ups, whose defining constraint is resource scarcity, the capacity to substitute intelligent software for labour, capital and time is therefore not a peripheral efficiency question but a core strategic capability (Csaszar & Steinberger, 2022).

India provides a compelling laboratory for studying these dynamics. The country hosts more than 1.57 lakh DPIIT-recognised start-ups that have collectively created over 1.66 million jobs, and its AI market is projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate of 25 to 35 per cent to reach approximately USD 17 billion by 2027 (Ministry of Finance, 2025; NASSCOM, 2023). National policy has reinforced this momentum: the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence articulates an #AIforAll vision (NITI Aayog, 2018), and the IndiaAI Mission, approved in March 2024, commits more than Rs. 10,300 crore over five years to compute capacity, data platforms and skilling. NITI Aayog estimates that AI could add USD 957 billion to India's economy by 2035, and management research increasingly frames AI as a source of business value that must be aligned with organisational routines to be realised (Enholm, Papagiannidis, Mikalef, & Krogstie, 2022).

Within India, Maharashtra occupies the leading position in the national start-up map. The state hosts more than 26,000 DPIIT-recognised start-ups, the largest share of any state, together with an estimated 15 to 17 unicorns, and its economy, with a gross state domestic product of roughly Rs. 42.7 lakh crore in 2024-25, is the largest among Indian states (DPIIT, 2025; Government of Maharashtra, 2025). The Maharashtra State Start-up Action Plan of 2018, the M-Hub platform and the Maharashtra State Innovation and Start-up Fund have collectively built an enabling infrastructure spanning incubation, seed support and market access (Government of Maharashtra, 2018). Yet the ecosystem remains spatially concentrated: Mumbai and Pune absorb the bulk of venture funding while Tier-II and Tier-III cities such as Nashik, Nagpur and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar are only beginning to participate. Whether AI technologies narrow or widen this spatial divide, and how far they translate into measurable growth and innovation outcomes for young firms, are questions that the existing literature has not answered with state-level evidence.

Three gaps motivate this study. First, the AI-business value literature is dominated by large-firm and advanced-economy samples, leaving the start-up context underexplored even though AI value creation mechanisms differ sharply where organisational slack is minimal (Davenport & Ronanki, 2018; Ransbotham et al., 2019). Second, Indian empirical work on digital entrepreneurship concentrates on national aggregates or the Bangalore ecosystem, while Maharashtra, the largest state ecosystem, lacks a systematic assessment (Nambisan, 2017; Autio, Nambisan, Thomas, & Wright, 2018). Third, existing studies rarely test group differences across sectors, funding stages and city tiers simultaneously, which limits the usefulness of their recommendations for differentiated policy. Addressing these gaps, the present study pursues five objectives:
(i) to assess the current level and pattern of AI technology adoption among Maharashtra start-ups across functional domains;
(ii) to examine the relationship between AI adoption and perceived start-up growth in revenue, employment and market terms;
(iii) to evaluate the influence of AI adoption on innovation capability and innovation output;
(iv) to compare adoption and growth outcomes across city tiers, sectors and funding stages; and
(v) to derive policy and managerial suggestions for deepening AI-led start-up growth in Maharashtra.
Consistent with these objectives and with the resource-based and dynamic-capabilities perspectives (Barney, 1991; Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997), four hypotheses are advanced:
H1. AI technology adoption is positively and significantly associated with the growth performance of Maharashtra start-ups.
H2. AI technology adoption is positively and significantly associated with the innovation capability of Maharashtra start-ups.
H3. The effect of AI adoption on growth outcomes differs significantly across sectors.
H4. AI adoption levels differ significantly between Tier-1 hub start-ups (Mumbai and Pune) and those located in Tier-II/III cities.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews the theoretical and empirical literature. Section 3 describes the research methodology. Section 4 presents the data analysis and results. Section 5 discusses the findings, Section 6 develops suggestions and implications, Section 7 acknowledges limitations, and Section 8 concludes.

subsections.heading: 2.1 Theoretical Foundations
paragraphs: Three complementary theoretical streams inform this study. The resource-based view holds that firms gain durable advantage from resources that are valuable, rare, inimitable and organisationally embedded (Barney, 1991). Data assets, trained models and AI-complementary routines increasingly satisfy these criteria, particularly for start-ups whose entire value proposition may rest on proprietary data feedback loops. The dynamic capabilities framework extends this logic to changing environments, emphasising sensing, seizing and reconfiguring as the capabilities through which firms convert technological opportunity into commercial outcomes (Teece et al., 1997). AI adoption is a paradigmatic seizing decision, and the speed with which young firms reconfigure processes around AI signals their dynamic capability. Finally, the diffusion of innovations tradition explains how adoption spreads through ecosystems via relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability (Rogers, 2003). Digital affordance theory refines this account for entrepreneurship, arguing that digital technologies relax spatial and resource constraints and thereby reshape ecosystem genesis (Nambisan, 2017; Autio et al., 2018). In the information systems tradition, digital business strategy research similarly treats technology infrastructure as a strategic capability whose value depends on how thoroughly it is woven into strategy and operations (Bharadwaj et al., 2013). Together these lenses predict that AI adoption should be uneven across sectors and locations, and that its payoff should operate through efficiency, customer engagement and innovation channels.

subsections.heading: 2.2 Global Evidence on AI and Firm Performance
paragraphs: Empirical research on the business value of AI has grown rapidly. An early global survey of 250 executives found that organisations adopt AI across four archetypes of process automation, cognitive insight, cognitive engagement and cognitive exploration, but that most firms pursue pilots rather than enterprise-wide deployment (Davenport & Ronanki, 2018). Cross-industry surveys likewise report a persistent gap between adoption ambition and realised value, with only a minority of firms scaling AI beyond isolated use cases (Ransbotham et al., 2019). A systematic literature review of 71 studies concludes that AI contributes to business value through operational, decisional and strategic mechanisms, but that value realisation depends on complementary assets such as data infrastructure, skills and top-management support (Enholm et al., 2022). Recent quasi-experimental evidence shows that access to a generative AI assistant raised support-agent productivity by about 14 per cent on average and by over 30 per cent for novice workers, demonstrating both the magnitude and the distributional character of AI gains (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025). Theoretical work further argues that AI reshapes organisational design itself by shifting the boundaries of hierarchy, delegation and coordination (Csaszar & Steinberger, 2022). Beyond commercial outcomes, AI is also positioned as an instrument for sustainable development when governance safeguards are present (Nishant, Kennedy, & Corbett, 2020).

subsections.heading: 2.3 Indian and Maharashtra-Specific Context
paragraphs: Indian institutional reports document rapid ecosystem expansion but less firm-level causal evidence. The National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence identified start-ups as critical bridge actors between research and application and recommended targeted support for AI entrepreneurship (NITI Aayog, 2018). NASSCOM (2023) estimates annual demand for roughly 6.29 lakh AI and machine-learning professionals against a supply of about 4.16 lakh, implying a talent gap that bears directly on start-up hiring capacity. The Economic Survey 2024-25 records continued acceleration in DPIIT recognitions and unicorns, while Maharashtra-specific assessments note the state's first rank in recognised start-ups, its strong incubator density in Mumbai and Pune, and emerging hubs in Nashik and Nagpur (Ministry of Finance, 2025; Government of Maharashtra, 2025). Entrepreneurial-ecosystem scholarship cautions that policy attention should focus on strengthening connective tissue, such as accelerators, angel networks and university linkages, rather than subsidising isolated firms (Isenberg, 2010). subsections.heading: 3.1 Research Design
paragraphs: The study adopts a descriptive-cum-causal research design that integrates secondary ecosystem data with primary survey evidence. The descriptive component profiles the Maharashtra start-up ecosystem between 2019 and 2025 using official recognition statistics, funding trackers and state economic documents. The causal component estimates associations between AI adoption and growth and innovation outcomes from a structured cross-sectional survey, supplemented by group comparisons across city tiers, sectors and funding stages. This combination allows the study to situate firm-level results within the observable trajectory of the ecosystem, strengthening external validity while preserving analytical tractability.

subsections.heading: 3.2 Population, Sample and Data Collection
paragraphs: The target population comprises founders, co-founders and senior managers of DPIIT-recognised start-ups headquartered in Maharashtra. Following the sample-size table of Krejcie and Morgan (1970) for a large finite population and adding a buffer for non-response, 480 questionnaires were distributed through incubation centres, industry associations and the M-Hub network using stratified purposive sampling across five cities: Mumbai, Pune, Nashik, Nagpur and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. A total of 428 responses were returned (89.2 per cent), of which 412 were complete and usable, yielding an effective response rate of 85.8 per cent. Data were collected between November 2025 and February 2026 through a mix of face-to-face and online administered questionnaires. Every respondent gave informed consent, and participation was voluntary and anonymous; the protocol follows institutional research-ethics guidelines.

subsections.heading: 3.3 Instrument and Measures
paragraphs: The instrument contained two parts. Part A captured demographic and organisational attributes: city, sector, funding stage, firm age, employment size and founder education. Part B measured five latent constructs on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). AI adoption (AIA, eight items) captured the extent of use of machine learning and predictive analytics, natural language processing and chatbots, generative AI tools, marketing automation, robotic process automation and computer vision. Operational efficiency (EFF, six items), customer engagement (CEN, six items), innovation capability (INN, six items) and growth performance (GRW, six items) captured outcome perceptions adapted from the AI business value literature (Davenport & Ronanki, 2018; Enholm et al., 2022). The full questionnaire appears in Appendix A. In addition, respondents reported actual revenue growth over the preceding financial year, which is used for the scatter analysis in Section 4.8.

subsections.heading: 3.4 Reliability and Validity
paragraphs: Internal consistency was assessed with Cronbach's alpha (Cronbach, 1951), and sampling adequacy with the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure and Bartlett's test of sphericity (Kaiser, 1974). As Table 2 shows, all constructs exceed the 0.70 threshold, and overall instrument reliability is 0.93. The KMO statistic of 0.874 is meritorious, and Bartlett's chi-square of 6,842.5 (df = 496, p < .001) confirms factorability. Exploratory factor analysis with varimax rotation reproduced the five intended factors with loadings above 0.55 and no substantial cross-loadings, supporting construct validity (Hair, Black, Babin, & Anderson, 2019).

subsections.heading: 3.5 Conceptual Framework and Statistical Tools
paragraphs: The conceptual framework in Figure 1 links AI technology adoption, the independent variable, to two dependent variables: start-up growth and innovation capability with output. Sector, city tier and funding stage are treated as moderating group factors, generating hypotheses H3 and H4. The baseline regression model estimated in Section 4.6 is specified in Eq. Analyses were conducted in SPSS (version 27) and comprise descriptive statistics, Pearson product-moment correlations, ordinary least squares multiple regression, independent-samples t-tests and one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc comparisons. Effect sizes are reported as Cohen's d and eta-squared, interpreted with conventional benchmarks (Cohen, 1988).

body.heading: 4. Data Analysis and Results
paragraphs: This section reports the empirical results in eight parts: the demographic profile of respondents, the macro trajectory of the Maharashtra ecosystem, patterns of AI usage, descriptive statistics of the constructs, correlation analysis, regression analysis, group comparisons addressing H3 and H4, and innovation output by AI maturity. All statistical tables use the conventional significance notations of p < .05, p < .01 and p < .001.

subsections.heading: 4.1 Demographic Profile of Respondents
paragraphs: Table 3 summarises the profile of the 412 respondent start-ups. The sample is geographically anchored in the two Tier-1 hubs of Mumbai (31.1 per cent) and Pune (28.6 per cent), with meaningful representation from Nashik, Nagpur and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar that allows the city-tier comparison required by H4. Sectorally, FinTech (22.3 per cent), D2C and e-commerce (20.9 per cent), HealthTech (18.9 per cent) and EdTech (18.0 per cent) dominate, followed by AgriTech and other technology ventures. The funding-stage distribution is balanced across bootstrapped, seed and series stages, and the majority of firms are less than five years old (78.6 per cent), consistent with the early-life focus of growth research. Post-graduate founders account for 51.5 per cent of the sample, underscoring the knowledge-intensive character of the ecosystem.

subsections.heading: 4.2 The Maharashtra Start-up Ecosystem, 2019-2025
paragraphs: Before turning to firm-level evidence, it is useful to anchor the analysis in the macro trajectory of the ecosystem. Table 4 compiles approximate indicators compiled from DPIIT recognition statistics, funding trackers and state economic documents (DPIIT, 2025; Government of Maharashtra, 2025). Cumulative DPIIT recognitions in the state grew from roughly 4,900 in 2019 to an estimated 26,400 in 2025, an almost 5.4-fold expansion that comfortably preserves Maharashtra's rank as the leading start-up state, ahead of Karnataka and Delhi, as visualised in Figure 2. Equity funding displayed a pronounced cycle, rising from about USD 2.1 billion in 2019 to a peak near USD 10.4 billion in 2022, correcting sharply during the 2023 funding winter to USD 4.3 billion, and then recovering to approximately USD 7.1 billion in 2025. The estimated share of AI-led start-ups among new recognitions climbed steadily from about 11 per cent to 27 per cent over the same window, indicating that the technology mix of the ecosystem is tilting decisively toward AI-native ventures.

subsections.heading: 4.3 Patterns of AI Technology Usage
paragraphs: Among the 412 respondents, 355 firms (86.2 per cent) reported deploying at least one AI technology in their core operations, confirming that AI has crossed the early-adopter threshold in the state's ecosystem. Figure 4 breaks down the primary use case of these adopters: customer service and support (26 per cent) and marketing and sales (24 per cent) together account for half of all primary deployments, followed by analytics and forecasting (19 per cent), operations and supply chain (14 per cent), finance and compliance (9 per cent) and product development (8 per cent). The functional pattern suggests that Maharashtra start-ups currently exploit AI most intensively at the customer interface, while deeper product-embedded uses remain comparatively rare, an observation consistent with the pilot-stage behaviour reported in the global literature (Davenport & Ronanki, 2018).

Table 5 and Figure 5 deepen this picture with technology-wise adoption rates and mean usage intensity on the five-point scale. Data analytics and business intelligence lead on both metrics (78.9 per cent adoption; M = 4.02), followed by marketing automation (71.4 per cent; M = 3.90) and chatbots or virtual assistants (66.7 per cent; M = 3.81). Generative AI tools, despite entering the market only recently, already rank fourth (61.2 per cent; M = 3.68), evidencing exceptionally fast diffusion (Rogers, 2003). In contrast, computer vision (28.2 per cent; M = 2.87) and robotic process automation (39.6 per cent; M = 3.12) trail the field, plausibly because they demand larger data and integration investments that young firms cannot yet commit.

subsections.heading: 4.4 Descriptive Statistics of the Constructs
paragraphs: Table 6 presents the descriptive statistics of the five study constructs. Customer engagement records the highest mean (M = 3.94, SD = 0.66), followed by operational efficiency (M = 3.89, SD = 0.63), growth performance (M = 3.78, SD = 0.68), innovation capability (M = 3.71, SD = 0.74) and AI adoption (M = 3.62, SD = 0.71). All distributions show small negative skewness and kurtosis values within the plus-minus one band, indicating approximate normality and the suitability of parametric testing (Hair et al., 2019). Substantively, the mean profile suggests that Maharashtra start-ups experience AI chiefly as a customer-facing and efficiency technology first, with growth and innovation gains arriving as adoption deepens. Respondents also reported an average actual revenue growth of 19.6 per cent (SD = 14.2) over the preceding financial year, which provides the outcome for the scatter analysis in Section 4.8.

subsections.heading: 4.5 Correlation Analysis
paragraphs: Table 7 reports the Pearson correlation matrix. AI adoption is positively and significantly associated with operational efficiency (r = .58), customer engagement (r = .61), innovation capability (r = .57) and growth performance (r = .62), all at p < .01, providing preliminary support for H1 and H2. The outcome constructs intercorrelate moderately, with innovation capability showing the strongest link to growth (r = .64), which anticipates the mediating role of innovation examined through the regression models below. The correlation magnitudes, ranging between .49 and .64, fall in the moderate band, indicating related but distinct constructs and no evidence of multicollinearity among predictors.

subsections.heading: 4.6 Regression Analysis
paragraphs: Two ordinary least squares regressions were estimated using the specification in Eq. (1). Model 1 regresses growth performance on AI adoption, the three channel constructs, funding access and firm age; Model 2 replaces the dependent variable with innovation capability to probe the innovation pathway. As Table 8 shows, Model 1 explains 48.7 per cent of the variance in growth (adjusted R-squared = 0.478), F(7, 404) = 54.79, p < .001. AI adoption emerges as the strongest predictor (beta = .316, t = 6.45, p < .001), followed by innovation capability (beta = .264, t = 5.50, p < .001), operational efficiency (beta = .189, t = 3.63, p < .001) and customer engagement (beta = .148, t = 2.90, p < .01). Funding access exerts a smaller positive influence (beta = .132, p < .01), while firm age is marginally negative, suggesting younger ventures extract growth benefits from AI more readily. Model 2 explains 41.2 per cent of the variance in innovation capability, F(5, 406) = 56.88, p < .001, with AI adoption again dominant (beta = .312, p < .001). Taken together, the models support H1 and H2 and indicate that AI adoption feeds growth both directly and through innovation and engagement channels.

subsections.heading: 4.7 Group Comparisons: City Tier, Sector and Funding Stage
paragraphs: Table 9 assembles the hypothesis tests for group differences. Panel A addresses H4 with an independent-samples t-test on the AI adoption index comparing Tier-1 hub firms (Mumbai and Pune, n = 246) with Tier-II/III firms (n = 166). Tier-1 firms score significantly higher (M = 3.72, SD = 0.66 versus M = 3.49, SD = 0.77), t(410) = 3.24, p = .001, with a small-to-moderate effect size (Cohen's d = 0.33), confirming H4 while also revealing that the spatial gap, though real, is modest in magnitude. Panel B tests H3 through one-way ANOVA of adoption across sectors, which yields a significant difference, F(5, 406) = 6.74, p < .001, eta-squared = .077. Tukey post-hoc comparisons show FinTech ventures scoring significantly above AgriTech (mean difference = 0.62, p < .001) and EdTech (mean difference = 0.36, p = .014), with HealthTech and D2C occupying intermediate positions; H3 is therefore supported. Panel C compares growth performance across funding stages and finds a clear monotonic gradient from bootstrapped firms (M = 3.51) to Series B and beyond (M = 4.06), F(3, 408) = 11.83, p < .001, eta-squared = .080. Figure 6 visualises the stage-wise profile across all five dimensions, showing that funded ventures outscore bootstrapped peers on every dimension even as the relative ordering of dimensions remains stable.
